name: Upland Cress
variety: Upland cress crop type; cultivar unspecified
summary: A cool-season leafy biennial grown for peppery greens. This entry represents the upland-cress crop type, not a named cultivar.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Barbarea verna in Brassicaceae and describes it as a biennial temperate species used for food. KSU Extension identifies upland cress as a leafy green; no cultivar is named here.

cultivation.short: Keep the leafy crop cool and evenly moist
cultivation.guidance: KSU Extension describes upland cress as a cool-season leafy green for fertile, moist, well-drained garden soil. The Royal Horticultural Society advises moist soil in full sun or partial shade. These are outdoor garden conditions; neither source defines indoor grow-light settings or hydroponic compatibility.

growth.short: Biennial rosette; RHS lists a broad 10–50 cm outdoor size range
growth.guidance: Kew classifies Barbarea verna as biennial. RHS describes a dark-green, deeply lobed rosette and lists 10–50 cm for both height and spread in UK garden conditions; treat that broad range as context, not a cultivar-specific prediction. In the second year it can produce upright flowering stems.

harvest.short: Harvest full rosettes at the basal plate or cut baby leaves above it
harvest.guidance: Johnny's cress growing guide gives separate harvest approaches for upland cress: cut full-size rosettes at the basal plate, or harvest baby leaves above it when they reach the desired size. Its thinning/row distances are outdoor soil guidance, not indoor pod spacing. This is crop-type guidance, not a cultivar-specific harvest age or regrowth guarantee.

problems.short: May be affected by flea beetle; RHS reports it is generally disease-free
problems.guidance: RHS lists possible flea-beetle susceptibility and describes the plant as generally disease-free in its garden profile. Treat this as a qualified source report, not a guarantee of pest absence or immunity in every region.

flowering.short: Yellow flowers are normal in the second year
flowering.guidance: RHS describes upright stems with clusters of small yellow flowers in spring or summer of the second year. This is normal biennial development; it is distinct from a first-year problem diagnosis.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected KSU guidance is for garden growing and does not validate hydroponic production.

evidence.note: RHS describes the species as a rosette; this does not imply a hydroponic footprint.

name: Jute Mallow
summary: A warm-season leafy crop also known as molokhia. Tropical field research documents repeated leaf harvest and shows that flowering can coincide with a shift away from vegetative leaf production; the exact response depends on harvest method and production context.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Corchorus olitorius in Malvaceae. The University of Minnesota source covers both C. olitorius and C. capsularis as jute mallow; this identity represents C. olitorius only, not both species as synonyms.

cultivation.short: Sunny sites, fertile soil, and abundant moisture are reported in Nigeria
cultivation.guidance: The University of Minnesota Plant Breeding Center describes full sun and fertile, well-drained soil for jute mallow. A Nigerian study of Corchorus olitorius for edible leaves also reports sunny sites, organic-rich soil, and abundant moisture. These are source-context growing conditions; neither source gives a numeric irrigation schedule or validates indoor/hydroponic production.

growth.short: Annual leafy herb grown for foliage
growth.guidance: Kew describes Corchorus olitorius as an annual. The Minnesota source identifies it as a leafy vegetable and fiber crop but also covers C. capsularis; dimensions and cultivar traits are not assigned to this record.

harvest.short: Repeated harvest is useful, but no universal interval is established
harvest.guidance: The University of Minnesota crop-group guide describes leaf or bunch harvest beginning around 40 days and then every two to three weeks through summer. A 2025 Niger field study of multiple Corchorus species found that the better harvest interval depended on both species and technique; its C. olitorius results varied between scraping and cutting. Treat both as regional production evidence, not a fixed home-garden calendar or cultivar guarantee.

flowering.short: Reproductive growth can compete with leaf-production goals
flowering.guidance: In a 2025 field study in Niger, leaf biomass was higher in plants from which flowers and fruits were removed under the study's production treatments. The experiment covered several Corchorus species and harvest methods, so this supports flowering as a relevant transition for leaf-focused production, not a universal deadheading prescription or guaranteed household yield response.

problems.short: Regional reports name leaf-feeding caterpillars, mites, and root-knot nematodes
problems.guidance: A 1988 Nigerian paper on Corchorus olitorius identifies caterpillars and mites feeding on leaves and Meloidogyne nematodes that reduce yield. These are risks reported in that production context, not a universal susceptibility claim. The paper does not provide a home-garden diagnostic or treatment protocol; it says diseases were few and not serious in its setting, which should not be generalized as disease resistance.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected source addresses soil growing and does not establish hydroponic suitability.

growthHabits.reason: A controlled growth habit for indoor system compatibility is not established.

height.reason: The source covers two species and does not establish a cultivar-specific height for this identity.

spread.reason: No relevant indoor mature spread is supported.

spacing.reason: Field spacing is not converted to hydroponic pod spacing.

light.reason: Full sun is an outdoor exposure statement, not an indoor grow-light classification.

name: Bottle Gourd
summary: A vigorous, night-flowering annual vine grown for edible young fruit and for mature hard-shelled gourds. It needs a warm, sunny outdoor site and room or strong support; no compact or hydroponic use is inferred.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Lagenaria siceraria in Cucurbitaceae and describes it as a climbing annual. Bottle, calabash and birdhouse are horticultural/product forms within the species; no named cultivar is established here.

cultivation.short: Full sun, consistent moisture and a warm growing season
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension describes full-sun cultivation in well-drained sandy or loamy soil with consistent moisture; the vine tolerates hot, humid summers and needs a long warm season for mature gourds. These are outdoor garden conditions, not an indoor or hydroponic recipe. Support the vine when growing ornamental gourds so fruit stays off the ground.

growth.short: Vigorous climbing vine with large flowers that open at night
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes an annual climbing vine with large white flowers opening at night and reports that hand pollination can enhance fruit set. UNH's 15–35-foot vine length is specific to its birdhouse-gourd context, not a universal dimension for every bottle-gourd form. This plant needs substantial outdoor room or support; no machine fit follows from the vine description.

harvest.short: Harvest young fruit for food or leave selected fruit to harden
harvest.guidance: NC State Extension describes young fruit as edible and says mature fruit is ready when its skin has hardened; mature shells may then be dried for containers, instruments or ornament. The source gives no cultivar-independent size or calendar for young-fruit harvest. A separate food-safety authority reports poisonings from bottle-gourd fruit with strong bitterness: do not consume fruit that tastes unusually bitter.

problems.short: Strong bitterness in the fruit is a food-safety warning
problems.guidance: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Food Safety Information Center reports bottle-gourd poisonings after ingestion of strongly bitter fruit and identifies cucurbitacin as the toxic constituent. Do not eat fruit with an unusual strong bitter taste. NC State also lists cucurbit pests and diseases, including cucumber beetles, squash bugs, vine borers and mildews; the profile does not claim cultivar resistance or prescribe a treatment.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected sources document outdoor soil cultivation, not hydroponic production.

growthHabits.reason: A vigorous climbing vine is documented, but the controlled vocabulary does not establish machine-system fit.

height.reason: Vine length is not equivalent to vertical plant height.

spread.reason: Long vine growth is not a finite mature spread value for a container or system.

spacing.reason: Outdoor spacing varies with vine training and is not a hydroponic pod-spacing recommendation.

light.reason: Full sun is documented outdoors but is not mapped to an indoor grow-light tier.
